paragraphs: This paper models how people move their eyes while searching for an object belonging to a particular category. The task involves locating a teddy bear among visually complicated objects. The model aims to reproduce the sequence of fixations leading to the target, connecting object recognition with the behavior used to find it.

The approach combines a computer vision detector with a biologically plausible model of eye movements. The detector uses SIFT features trained with AdaBoost, while the eye movement component generates simulated fixations. Together, these components provide a way to study how information useful for recognizing a target can guide a sequence of looks through a scene.

The authors compare the model with human observers performing the same search task. They report considerable agreement in the number of fixations, the cumulative probability of looking at the target, and scanpath distance. Agreement across these measures supports the model as an account of several aspects of search behavior in the studied task.
neurips-2005-a-computational-model-of-ey.tldr: A model combining object detection and eye movement mechanisms reproduces several measures of human visual search behavior.

paragraphs: This paper proposes accelerating manifold learning by dividing the sample points into two subdomains. Rather than handling the entire collection as one embedding problem, the approach works with embeddings of the two pieces. The central question is how to combine those local results into an embedding of the full collection.

The authors develop a solution to the interface problem between the subdomains. This interface supplies the mechanism for gluing their embeddings together. Its importance is that separately constructed representations must fit together coherently: obtaining two local embeddings is only part of the work required to produce a useful representation of the whole domain.

The paper also analyzes errors introduced by this joining process using matrix perturbation theory. That analysis makes the consequences of decomposition an explicit part of the method, alongside its computational motivation. Numerical examples illustrate the proposed approach's efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines a divide-and-combine algorithm with an assessment of the errors associated with assembling its results.
neurips-2005-a-domain-decomposition-meth.tldr: The method accelerates manifold learning by joining embeddings of two subdomains and analyzing the errors introduced by that joining.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent a signal using as few elements as possible from a redundant dictionary. Because the dictionary offers overlapping ways to express the signal, finding a valid representation does not by itself establish that it is maximally sparse. The authors investigate when sparse Bayesian learning, or SBL, recovers that sparsest representation.

Their main theoretical result gives a restricted equivalence condition determined by the distribution of the nonzero weights generating the signal. When that condition holds, the SBL solution equals the maximally sparse representation. They also prove that drawing those weights from an approximate Jeffreys prior satisfies the condition with probability approaching one. This connects recovery behavior to assumptions about the generating weights.

The authors additionally motivate a worst-case scenario for SBL and demonstrate better performance there than Basis Pursuit and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit. These results strengthen their argument for SBL while retaining a distinction between conditional recovery guarantees and the comparative performance demonstrated in the paper.
neurips-2005-comparing-the-effects-of-di.tldr: The paper establishes weight-distribution conditions under which sparse Bayesian learning recovers a maximally sparse signal representation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for learning object-category templates that support both recognition and localization. Recognizing a category means identifying the kind of object present; localization additionally identifies where it appears. The method connects these goals through a model of how an object's parts are arranged and how those parts produce image features.

The generative model describes multiple parts relative to an object coordinate system. Its computational complexity grows slowly enough with the number of features to make training substantially more efficient than the compared methods. A variational approximation further accelerates learning, allowing the model to incorporate many more features while reducing training time by orders of magnitude relative to previous approaches.

The authors report that these computational changes also improve accuracy and localization. Tests on standard datasets compare the approach with recent template models and demonstrate results described as state of the art for detection and localization. The contribution links efficient learning with a richer feature representation and reported improvements in both recognition tasks.
neurips-2005-efficient-unsupervised-lear.tldr: An efficient generative model of object parts enables faster learning with more features and improves reported detection and localization results.

paragraphs: Lasso regression can select features by assigning zero weight to many irrelevant or redundant inputs. The paper addresses its restriction to linear models. Extending feature selection to nonlinear relationships is challenging because kernel methods that scale features can require difficult, nonconvex optimization.

The proposed Feature Vector Machine starts by rewriting standard Lasso in a form structurally equivalent to a support vector machine. This reformulation permits a nonlinear extension through kernels defined on feature vectors. The resulting method produces sparse solutions in the nonlinear feature space and is described as substantially more tractable than kernel machines based on feature scaling.

Experiments on simulated data give encouraging results for identifying a small number of dominant features whose relationships with the response are nonlinear. Standard Lasso fails to complete that task in the reported experiments. The significance is the route from a familiar linear selection method to a nonlinear one: changing the formulation makes kernels available while preserving a sparse representation.
neurips-2005-from-lasso-regression-to-fe.tldr: The Feature Vector Machine reformulates Lasso to enable tractable kernel-based selection of features with nonlinear relationships to the response.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether clustering objects using only some of their attributes can reveal meaningful structure in attributes that were never observed. The setting involves objects described by many attributes, with clustering performed on a relatively small random subset. The desired generalization is therefore across attributes, rather than simply to additional objects.

The authors show that, under mild technical conditions, clustering from this random subset performs almost as well as clustering from the full attribute collection. They establish finite-sample generalization theorems for this learning scheme, extending analogous ideas from supervised learning. The random selection of attributes and the stated technical conditions are part of the setting supporting that conclusion.

A collaborative-filtering demonstration treats users as objects and movie ratings as attributes. In this setting, the result concerns whether groupings based on some ratings can capture information about other ratings. The paper gives theoretical support for learning useful group structure from partial attribute information, alongside an application illustrating what generalization to unobserved features means.
neurips-2005-generalization-in-clusterin.tldr: Under mild technical conditions, clustering on a small random subset of attributes performs almost as well as using all attributes.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix approximation represents nonnegative data through a smaller set of nonnegative factors. Such representations can be sparse and describe data in terms of component parts, making them useful for dimensionality reduction and analysis. This paper focuses on improving the algorithms used to compute those factors.

The authors formulate generalized approximation problems using Bregman divergences to measure the mismatch between an input matrix and its low-rank approximation. They derive multiplicative update algorithms for solving these problems. Previously established multiplicative updates arise as a special case, so the framework broadens the available objectives while retaining a connection to existing methods.

The paper also explains how penalty functions can incorporate constraints beyond nonnegativity. It discusses extensions using link functions to model nonlinear relationships. Together, these developments make the approximation framework more adaptable: the discrepancy measure, additional constraints, and relationship between the representation and the data can be modeled more flexibly. The stated contribution is primarily algorithmic, expanding how nonnegative approximations can be formulated and computed.
neurips-2005-generalized-nonnegative-mat.tldr: The paper generalizes nonnegative matrix approximation through Bregman-divergence objectives, multiplicative updates, and additional modeling constraints.

paragraphs: This paper treats imitation as a problem of understanding another agent's goal and choosing actions to achieve it. The proposed framework uses a learned probabilistic graphical model of the environment. Within that model, uncertainty about what a teacher intends can be handled alongside the problem of deciding what the learner should do.

The authors first develop planning algorithms that use probabilistic inference to find actions leading to a goal state. Planning then helps initiate the learning of policies conditioned on goals, with feedback from the environment supporting that learning. This connects an ability to plan for an explicit goal with an ability to act toward goals inferred from observation.

A simple maze-navigation task illustrates the resulting imitation behavior. The agent can infer a teacher's goals and imitate the teacher even when the demonstration is incomplete and the goals remain uncertain. The demonstration supports the framework's capacity for goal-based imitation in that setting, showing how planning, learning, and interpreting demonstrations can share one probabilistic representation.
neurips-2005-goal-based-imitation-as-pro.tldr: A learned graphical model enables an agent to infer a teacher's goals and plan imitative actions despite incomplete demonstrations.

paragraphs: Hot Coupling is a sampling method for undirected graphical models with pairwise interactions and arbitrary connectivity. It addresses both approximate inference and estimation of the partition function, the normalization quantity needed to turn the model's weights into probabilities. These tasks become difficult when the graph contains many interacting relationships.

The method uses sequential Monte Carlo, constructing a series of intermediate distributions that approach the desired distribution. It begins with samples drawn exactly from a spanning-tree model. It then progressively couples individual pairs of variables, introducing relationships through the sequence instead of controlling the transition solely by lowering a global temperature parameter.

The distinctive contribution is this construction of the intermediate targets. It organizes the journey from a tractable starting model to the desired model around individual pairwise couplings. The authors present experiments involving both sparse and densely connected graphs, examining inference and partition-function estimation. These experiments evaluate the two intended uses of the method across different patterns of graph connectivity.
neurips-2005-hot-coupling-a-particle-app.tldr: Hot Coupling uses sequential Monte Carlo to approach a pairwise graphical model by progressively coupling variables from a spanning-tree starting point.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the smallest region containing at least a specified amount of probability. Size is measured using a known reference measure, while probability comes from an unknown distribution. Such regions summarize concentrated probability mass and can support anomaly detection or the construction of confidence regions.

The available information consists of independent samples from the unknown distribution. The authors introduce estimation rules analogous to empirical risk minimization and structural risk minimization in classification. Their analysis connects performance to how uniformly sample-based probabilities approximate true probabilities across the candidate family of sets. This makes the complexity of that family central to the guarantees.

The paper derives finite-sample performance bounds involving VC dimension and related quantities. It also establishes strong universal consistency and an oracle inequality, providing additional theoretical guarantees for the estimators. Histogram-based estimators and dyadic partitions illustrate the rules. The contribution translates familiar learning-theory principles into a method for estimating compact probability regions from samples.
neurips-2005-learning-minimum-volume-set.tldr: The paper develops sample-based estimators of minimum-volume probability regions with finite-sample bounds and consistency guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper considers classification problems where the output contains several interdependent variables. Predicting such an output requires accounting for relationships among its components. The authors study this structured prediction problem in a semi-supervised setting, where unlabeled input examples are available alongside the information used for supervised learning.

Their discriminative approach uses the intrinsic geometry of the input patterns revealed by unlabeled points. Those points contribute information about how the inputs are organized, even though they do not supply labeled structured outputs. The authors incorporate this geometric information into a maximum-margin formulation for predicting structured variables.

A stated feature of the formulation is that it naturally applies to new test points. This extends its use beyond assigning predictions to a fixed collection of unlabeled examples, as in a transductive formulation. The contribution brings together output dependencies, input geometry, and maximum-margin learning in one framework, making unlabeled data part of the construction of a predictor that can subsequently process new inputs.
neurips-2005-maximum-margin-semi-supervi.tldr: The paper combines unlabeled-data geometry with maximum-margin structured prediction in a formulation that extends to new test points.

paragraphs: This paper studies resource allocation on sparse graphs, with task redistribution providing the problem context. The allocation variables are real-valued, so the problem concerns quantities that can vary continuously. The graph supplies the structure within which allocation is studied, making the relationships between connected parts of the system relevant to the solution.

The authors use methods from statistical physics to analyze the problem. Insights from that analysis then guide the design of an efficient distributed algorithm. The title identifies message passing as the computational approach. A central contribution is therefore the connection between a theoretical treatment of allocation and an algorithm organized for distributed computation on the graph.

Numerical simulations examine the resulting algorithm. The authors report excellent performance and full agreement between the simulations and their theoretical results. This agreement supports the link between the analysis and the implemented procedure in the investigated setting. The paper's stated outcome combines an effective allocation algorithm with numerical evidence that its behavior matches the theory used to develop it.
neurips-2005-message-passing-for-task-re.tldr: Statistical-physics analysis yields a distributed resource-allocation algorithm whose simulated behavior agrees with the theory.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why the receptive-field size of cells in primary visual cortex changes with contrast. A receptive field describes the spatial region influencing a cell's response. The authors examine this phenomenon using a large-scale spiking-neuron model of macaque V1 input layers, seeking mechanisms within the modeled neural interactions.

The simulations reveal a variety of mechanisms, which the authors analyze through the relative gains of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs. This directs attention to the balance of influences that promote or suppress a response. The model also shows that excitation and inhibition extend over larger spatial regions on average at low contrast, matching a prediction of phenomenological models.

However, the simulations suggest that this spatial expansion is neither sufficient nor necessary to explain the receptive-field effect. Observing expansion alone therefore does not establish the explanation, and the phenomenon need not require it within the model. The findings favor examining the interaction of excitation and inhibition rather than treating their spatial extent as a complete account.
neurips-2005-neural-mechanisms-of-contra.tldr: A spiking-neuron model suggests multiple mechanisms for contrast-dependent receptive fields, beyond expansion of excitation and inhibition alone.

paragraphs: The paper modifies diffusion tensor MRI to delineate neuronal fibers in brain regions infiltrated by edema. The central issue addressed is contamination from free water, which affects the diffusion signal used to identify fibers. The method aims to separate that contribution before assessing the directional properties associated with the remaining tissue compartment.

The authors use a Multiple Tensor Variational framework, replacing the usual diffusion model with a model containing multiple components. They estimate the free-water volume fraction in each voxel, remove its contribution, and calculate the anisotropy of the remaining compartment. Variational regularization supports fitting this more complex model to the measured signal attenuation.

The framework is applied to data acquired with conventional clinical parameters and only six diffusion directions. The authors report that regularization enables them to overcome the highly ill-posed fitting problem in this setting. Their results identify fibers that conventional diffusion tensor MRI did not find, supporting the usefulness of explicitly modeling free-water contamination in the studied edema data.
neurips-2005-neuronal-fiber-delineation-.tldr: A regularized multicomponent diffusion model removes estimated free-water contamination and reveals fibers missed by conventional diffusion tensor MRI.

paragraphs: The two-thirds power law describes an inverse nonlinear relationship between movement speed and trajectory curvature. Its appearance in movement and perception has motivated explanations based on smoothness or mechanisms that suppress motor noise. This paper examines whether noise itself can produce the relationship, changing how evidence for those explanations should be interpreted.

The authors show that white Gaussian noise obeys the power law. They also combine noise with synthetic trajectories deliberately constructed to violate it, finding that low noise levels can make those trajectories comply. Some types of colored noise have a similar effect that persists despite smoothing, so smoothing does not necessarily remove the influence they identify.

These findings motivate careful noise analysis in experiments testing the law. Observing the relationship may reflect properties of the noise as well as properties of the underlying movement. The authors also suggest that correlated motor noise could contribute to the law's origin. They present this as a possible explanation, rather than establishing it as the cause of human movement behavior.
neurips-2005-noise-and-the-two-thirds-po.tldr: Noise can produce the two-thirds power law, suggesting caution when interpreting it as evidence for movement-smoothing mechanisms.

paragraphs: This paper studies recognizing an object from a single image by learning useful variation from other objects. A labeled reference collection provides examples of changes in pose, illumination, and noise. The learned information is then used to judge whether two images depict the same new object, even though that object was absent from training.

The proposed chopping scheme makes hundreds of random binary divisions of the reference set. Each division keeps all images of a given object together. A simple learning algorithm extends each division to the wider image space, producing predictors that can respond to previously unseen images.

For a pair of images, the method combines those predictors' responses using a Bayesian rule to obtain a posterior probability of similarity. The authors evaluate the scheme on COIL-100 and a collection of 150 degraded LaTeX symbols. They compare it with learning from several positive examples and with learning similarity directly. The approach's central contribution is a mechanism for transferring knowledge about appearance variation into recognition from one example.
neurips-2005-pattern-recognition-from-on.tldr: Chopping learns random object-preserving partitions of reference images and combines them to judge similarity between images of unseen objects.

paragraphs: The paper addresses planning when tasks can overlap, take time to finish, have uncertain outcomes, and compete for limited resources. A useful policy must decide how to act under these interacting conditions. Such problems are commonly modeled as Markov decision problems, but the authors focus on domains too large for dynamic programming to be feasible.

Their approach applies reinforcement learning through a policy-gradient method. They construct a simple policy, or agent, for each planning task. This produces a factored representation of the planner, organizing its behavior around individual tasks while using policy-gradient learning to improve the resulting choices.

The resulting system, called the Factored Policy-Gradient Planner, can handle hundreds of tasks. It optimizes criteria involving success probability, duration, and resource use. The contribution demonstrates that policy-gradient methods can support probabilistic temporal planning at this scale. Its significance is the combination of task-level policies with learning in domains where concurrency, uncertainty, and resource limits make planning computationally demanding.
neurips-2005-policy-gradient-methods-for.tldr: The Factored Policy-Gradient Planner learns task-level policies for large temporal planning problems involving uncertainty, concurrency, and limited resources.

paragraphs: This paper develops approximation techniques for undirected probabilistic graphical models by drawing on graphical preconditioners from scientific computing. The targets include event probabilities and the log partition function, which concerns the model's normalization. The framework supplies rigorous upper and lower bounds on these quantities through non-iterative procedures with low time complexity.

The approximations are constructed using tractable subgraphs, sharing that starting point with mean-field approaches. The distinctive step is to reformulate the choice of tractable distribution parameters and approximate inference as a matrix-preconditioning problem. This creates a connection between probabilistic approximation and established methods for working with linear systems.

The significance of the bounds is that the output includes controlled limits on the quantities of interest, rather than only approximate values. The non-iterative construction also makes computational cost part of the contribution. Experiments compare the proposed schemes with variational methods. Together, the framework and comparisons investigate whether tools developed for numerical computation can provide useful, rigorously bounded approximations for graphical models.
neurips-2005-preconditioner-approximatio.tldr: Graphical preconditioners provide efficient, non-iterative upper and lower bounds on probabilities and log partition functions.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether linear models can reconstruct muscle activity recorded during monkey arm movements from neural activity in primary motor cortex, or M1. High-dimensional recordings make ordinary regression numerically fragile and vulnerable to overfitting. The authors therefore develop a Bayesian approach to obtain a more robust analysis of the neural-to-muscle relationship.

Their regression method automatically identifies and excludes irrelevant input features. This feature selection also regularizes the model against overfitting. They compare it with ordinary least squares, stepwise regression, partial least squares, Lasso, and a brute-force search for predictive feature subsets, assessing a combination of computational efficiency, usability, and resistance to overfitting.

The authors report a superior mixture of those characteristics, supporting the method's potential as a replacement for other linear regression techniques. Their neuroscience analysis also finds that M1 activity predicts EMG data well. This supports the usefulness of linear prediction in the studied recordings and points toward possible real-time brain-machine interfaces, without presenting that application as already established.
neurips-2005-predicting-emg-data-from-m1.tldr: Bayesian linear regression selects relevant neural features and predicts muscle activity while offering a favorable balance of robustness, efficiency, and usability.

paragraphs: Rodeo addresses regression when many input variables are available but the unknown function satisfies a sparsity condition. It combines two decisions: which variables matter and how much smoothing to apply along each input direction. Making these decisions together allows the regression procedure to adapt its attention to relevant parts of a high-dimensional input.

The method gradually decreases bandwidths in directions where the estimator changes strongly with bandwidth. It uses a sequence of hypothesis tests to guide these reductions. This sensitivity-based mechanism connects variable selection to the behavior of the regression estimator itself, rather than treating selection as a separate preliminary operation.

Under the stated sparsity condition, the authors show that rodeo avoids the curse of dimensionality and achieves the optimal minimax convergence rate up to logarithmic factors, as though the relevant variables were known beforehand. The guarantee is conditional on that sparsity. A modified version uses soft rather than hard thresholding and effectively solves a sequence of Lasso problems, linking the procedure to another approach to sparse estimation.
neurips-2005-rodeo-sparse-nonparametric-.tldr: Rodeo jointly selects variables and smoothing bandwidths, achieving near-optimal regression rates under a sparsity condition.

paragraphs: This paper proposes separating mixed music signals by modeling their harmonic structure. The underlying idea is that a music signal has a stable harmonic organization that can be represented by a model. That stability provides information for distinguishing signals that overlap in a recording, a useful capability for tasks such as audio content analysis.

The algorithm learns a harmonic-structure model for each signal in the mixture. It then uses the models to distinguish the harmonic structures associated with the different signals and separate them. The approach therefore makes the modeled organization of the sources central to the separation process, with stability of that organization supplying its stated rationale.

The authors report successful separation with very high signal-to-noise ratio and good subjective audio quality. These findings address both a numerical measure of the recovered signals and how the resulting audio sounds. They provide experimental support for harmonic-structure modeling as a separation strategy in the evaluated setting, connecting the proposed representation with useful recovered music signals.
neurips-2005-separation-of-music-signals.tldr: The method separates music mixtures using learned harmonic-structure models, with reported high signal-to-noise ratios and good perceived audio quality.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks directions that capture substantial data variance while using only a limited number of variables. Enforcing that limit creates a nonconvex, NP-hard optimization problem. This paper approaches the selection directly through a discrete spectral formulation, complementing approaches that replace the hard constraint with continuous approximations or convex relaxations.

The formulation uses variational eigenvalue bounds to support two kinds of algorithms. A greedy strategy provides an approximate solution, while branch-and-bound search yields provably optimal solutions. The bounds therefore serve both practical search and exact optimization, connecting the spectral objective with decisions about which variables to include.

The exact methodology also reveals a simple renormalization step that improves approximate solutions produced by continuous methods. This makes part of the contribution useful beyond the proposed discrete algorithms themselves. Experiments on real-world benchmark data and extensive Monte Carlo trials demonstrate performance gains for the discrete approaches. The paper combines exact solution machinery, a greedy alternative, and a refinement for existing approximate solutions.
neurips-2005-spectral-bounds-for-sparse-.tldr: Spectral bounds enable greedy and provably optimal sparse PCA algorithms, while also yielding a refinement for continuous approximations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a scalable training algorithm for structured prediction with large margins. The models include an important class of Markov networks and combinatorial models, where outputs have internal relationships. The computational challenge is to estimate such models efficiently while preserving the structure that makes their predictions meaningful.

The authors formulate estimation as a convex-concave saddle-point problem and apply the extragradient method. The resulting algorithm uses gradient calculations and projections and has linear convergence. The projection operation can be solved with combinatorial algorithms for minimum-cost quadratic flow, providing a concrete computational route for this otherwise potentially demanding step.

This formulation offers an efficient alternative to approaches that reduce estimation to a quadratic program. Experiments examine two substantially different applications: three-dimensional image segmentation and word alignment. The authors report favorable scaling behavior across these tasks. The contribution links a saddle-point view of learning with tractable optimization operations, and the experiments illustrate its applicability across distinct kinds of structured outputs.
neurips-2005-structured-prediction-via-t.tldr: An extragradient algorithm trains large-margin structured models through gradient and flow-based projection operations with linear convergence.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a kernel method for extracting semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text. The target is the relationship expressed by the language surrounding or connecting the entities. The method uses a generalization of subsequence kernels to represent the textual patterns relevant to that decision.

The kernel incorporates three types of subsequence patterns commonly used in language to assert relationships between two entities. This makes the representation sensitive to recurring ways that text communicates a relation. The central design choice is to build these relation-oriented patterns into the kernel, so that they contribute directly to the method's assessment of textual examples.

Experiments investigate protein-interaction extraction from biomedical corpora and top-level relation extraction from newspaper corpora. The authors report advantages for their approach in these evaluations. These two applications show the method being used with both specialized scientific text and news text. The contribution is a relation-focused extension of subsequence kernels, supported by experiments in two different textual settings.
neurips-2005-subsequence-kernels-for-rel.tldr: A generalized subsequence kernel uses three types of linguistic patterns to extract relations between entities in biomedical and newspaper text.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find groups of observed points that fit an underlying model when the observations are dense and noisy. Its motivating application is linking faint asteroid detections. The broader computational problem is to identify compatible sets of points efficiently within a collection containing many observations that need not belong together.

The authors survey tree-based search approaches and identify a trade-off between algorithms using a single tree and those using multiple trees. They then introduce a multiple-tree algorithm that uses a variable number of trees. This variable choice is intended to exploit advantages from both existing approaches within one search method.

Experiments on simulated and astronomical data show that the proposed algorithm performs well. The use of both kinds of data connects the algorithmic idea to its motivating application while also testing it on constructed observations. The contribution is an adaptable tree-based search strategy for model-consistent point sets, with potential applicability to a range of spatial queries.
neurips-2005-variable-kd-tree-algorithms.tldr: A spatial-search algorithm varies its number of trees to combine advantages of single-tree and multiple-tree methods.
